name: Segregation
miniText: The scientific question is whether mild local similarity preferences can produce strong residential separation. In NetLogo's Segregation model, two agent types relocate when their neighboring same-type share falls below a specified satisfaction threshold. The selected literature connects this mechanism to micro-to-macro residential sorting: local preferences generate aggregate segregation without central coordination [1]; economic extensions test how additional incentives change segregation dynamics [2]; social context limits interpretation of physically similar spatial patterns [3]. Binary types and unrestricted relocation omit discrimination, housing costs and institutional constraints; local satisfaction is a stipulated rule rather than a measured universal preference. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

verification.evidenceSummary: A recent article [Vinkovic D, Kirman A (2006) Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 103:19261–19265] showing that the Schelling model has a physical analogue extends our understanding of the model. However, prior research has already outlined a mathematical basis for the Schelling model and simulations based on it have already enhanced our understanding of the social dynamics that underlie the model, something that the physical analogue does not address. Research in social science has provided a formal basis for the segregative outcomes resulting from the residential selection process and simulations have replicated relevant spatial outcomes under different specifications of the residential dynamics. New and increasingly detailed survey data on preferences demonstrates the embeddedness of the Schelling selection process in the social behaviors of choosing alternative residential compositions.
